Stated Claim / Post Context:
Let's pick apart Albo's excuses for his Helen Haines dirt file. The PM's spin is both outrageous and depressing: PETER VAN ONSELEN

Being Prime Minister is about doing three things well all at once: managing the politics, developing good policies and showing national leadership. Anthony Albanese excels at one of these.

Actual Article Body:
Published:  13:24 AEDT, 22 October 2026   |  Updated:  17:05 AEDT, 22 October 2026

Being Prime Minister is about doing three things well all at once: managing the politics, developing good policies and showing national leadership.

Anthony Albanese excels at one of these. Unfortunately for the rest of us, it's the one most useful for keeping him in the job, but the least useful for getting things done.

Albo defeated Scott Morrison in 2022, then secured a thumping majority at the next election in 2025. The fractured right wing has only strengthened his position. Despite his mid-term blues he'll probably do it again in 18 months' time.

You can argue about the quality of his opponents, but winning is winning. Albo has earned his place in Labor's electoral history. He's mastered the politics, and is within reach of Bob Hawke's record as Labor's longest serving PM.

The problem is what Albo does with his victories. Not much.

On policy, his government increasingly resembles a renovation where nobody checked the plans before knocking down the walls. Case in point: the latest Budget, its broken promises on negative gearing and capital gains taxes and the subsequent ATO and credit card surcharges debacle that followed.

Winning an election by misleading voters, then doing what you reassured them you wouldn't do is hardly an achievement to gloat about.

Albo's signature policy from his first term offers an even bigger moment of failure. He made the Voice referendum the defining moral project of his prime ministership, then failed at the essential task of bringing Australians with him for the ride.

Albo pressed ahead without bipartisan agreement and never adequately resolved the public's questions about how it would all work. The result was a crushing defeat at the referendum: more than 60 per cent of Australians voted No, with the referendum defeated in every single state.

Then there is Albo's (lack of) leadership. Perhaps his biggest failure so far. Two moments of national horror have exposed the limitations that electoral success often conceals when a leader isn't up to the task.

After the Bondi terror attack, Australians needed empathy, moral clarity and a willingness to accept responsibility. It was NSW Premier Chris Minns who supplied all of that in spades. Albo did not.

Helen Haines had taken aim at Albanese for his government's $6million grant for Marrickville Golf Club. Above, the Prime Minister is seen at Lewis the cavoodle's birthday party. Lewis is on right, Albanese's dog Toto is on the left

Minns acknowledged that his government should have done more. He stood before a grieving community and accepted responsibility for failing to protect it. He supported a royal commission while Albo resisted a national inquiry until he was eventually forced to relent.

The contrast between the pair was devastating precisely because both men wore Labor colours.

Minns understood that admitting failure could establish the trust needed to lead going forward. Albo seemed more preoccupied with how much failure he might be required to admit to.

Now we have the appalling attack on Helen Haines, the much loved independent MP.

The PM has rightly praised Haines' character and public service. Yet his response has been compromised by his refusal to properly address the dirt sheet that we revealed his own office circulated about her, just weeks earlier.

The document used her funding requests and personal connections to insinuate wrongdoing without a shred of evidence. It emerged after she criticised the $6 million grant for the Prime Minister's local golf club.

Asked whether he knew about or approved of its distribution, Albo instead explained that Haines was a good local member who advocated strongly for her community.

Exactly. So why was his office briefing against her for doing it? He won't explain that contradiction.

Perhaps because the PM, or someone very senior within his camp, directed the dirt unit to dig in the first place.

Then, Albo told the ABC that his office was simply sharing 'a list of funding from Helen Haines, just showing that people of integrity stand up for their electorate.'

'No personal criticism of Helen. Helen is a strong advocate for her electorate. She's advocated for funding for projects in her electorate,' he said.

The dirt file does contain a list of projects Haines was barracking for. But it's also a dirt sheet laden with innuendo.

It questions her integrity, disclosures and motives when lobbying for funding.

It also just so happened to be released immediately after Haines criticised the Albanese government's $6million grant to Marrickville Golf Club, which the PM is an honorary member of.

Not exactly the time for Albanese's office to put out a document highlighting Haines's integrity! (You can read the full file yourself at the bottom of this story.)

At issue here is Albanese's credibility when he calls for higher standards while declining to account for the conduct of his own office. Potentially at his direction.

The culture of a prime ministerial office is ultimately the Prime Minister's responsibility.

Instead, we get another demonstration of his instinct to find a (non)answer that gets him through an interview rather than confronts the problem in order to address it.

Albo has mastered the politics of becoming Prime Minister and remaining Prime Minister.

He's an electoral success, there is no doubt about that.

But is that really enough?
